title: Funerals in the code
hookLine: cremation, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas, a reading of the Granth, and no monuments

lines: THE SAME WORDS AT THE PYRE.
CLOSING A DAY, CLOSING A LIFE.
cards: There's a prayer Sikhs say at night, just before sleep. It's called Kirtan Sohila, it's short, and in some homes children grow up hearing it at bedtime, lights low, the day being put away.
Now the same words in a different place. A crematorium, or an open pyre. A family standing close together.
The body has been bathed and dressed. And the same bedtime prayer is said over it. The words that close an ordinary day are the words that close a life.

teach.b: The Sikh Rehat Maryada lays out a funeral in a few plain steps. In paraphrase: the body is bathed and clothed, and if the person was initiated, the five articles of faith stay with them.
The body is cremated; where cremation isn't possible, the code allows other means.
On the way and at the pyre, hymns are sung, Kirtan Sohila is recited when the fire is lit, and Ardas is said.

teach.h: A READING OF THE GRANTH, NO MONUMENT.
teach.b: Then a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib begins, at home or in a gurdwara, and when it's complete there's a bhog, the closing we met not long ago. Notice what the code leaves out.
It discourages loud wailing and breast-beating, and rejects rituals that grew up around death outside the Guru's teaching. It asks that no monument be built where the body was cremated. Why so plain?

In Sikh teaching a death happens within the hukam, God's order, the same order that gave the life. Grief is real, and the Gurus wrote about it; but the goodbye turns the family toward the Word instead of a stone.
The ashes aren't enshrined. The reading of the Granth is the memorial. That's why Kirtan Sohila fits: the prayer of going to rest, of a day returned to the One who gave it.
Said at the pyre, it meets death as the last evening, with the same words as every other.
A simple goodbye isn't a cold one. Nothing stands between the mourners and the Guru.

how: At a Sikh funeral the body is bathed, dressed and cremated while hymns are sung; Kirtan Sohila and Ardas are recited, a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib follows, and no monument is raised where the body was cremated.

games.q: what does “funerals in the code” mean?
o: a year of mourning in white, with daily wailing
cremation, Kirtan Sohila and a Granth reading, no monument
burial beside the gurdwara, under a carved headstone

games.q: a Sikh family wants to honor someone who has died. what does the code point them toward?
o: a stone shrine over the ashes.
a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.
games.why: the code begins a reading of the Granth and asks for no monument. the Word is the memorial.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has died, or someone you've had to let go of, and without reliving the whole story, ask what few plain words would be enough for a goodbye: a single line, maybe only their name, said once.
Hold those words, or say Waheguru once for them if you pray, and if the memory gets heavy, it's fine to stop and simply breathe.
If grief ever turns toward hurting yourself, please reach out now: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Funerals in the code. Cremation, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas at the pyre, a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and no monument. Today's word.
